reason: The aziridine ring geometry is essentially conserved across the set: N–C and C–C dimensions show no conspicuous ring distortion, so the ranking is controlled mainly by the hydroxymethyl orientation and the two carbon-chain torsions. First, the most favorable structures place O near N and direct the hydroxyl proton toward the amine lone-pair side. Conformers 10, 15, 14, 18, and 22 combine this contact with an extended, approximately anti terminal chain; their H···N distances are about 2.22–2.35 Å and O···N about 2.74–2.84 Å. Conformer 10 has the best overall combination of short H···N contact, good approach to the N lone-pair direction, and an extended chain. Conformers 15, 14, and 18 are very close; 15 has favorable lone-pair-side approach, while 14 has a slightly shorter H···N distance. Conformer 22 retains the anti chain but has a somewhat longer donor–acceptor contact. Second, conformers 29, 12, 7, 16, 23, and 9 also have productive O–H···N arrangements but place the terminal carbon chain in a gauche state, indicated by terminal-C-to-central-C separations near 3.2 Å rather than about 3.9 Å for the extended structures. Conformer 29 is best in this subgroup because the H approaches the amine lone-pair direction particularly well; 12 has a similarly short H···N distance. The gauche penalty makes this subgroup slightly less favorable than the hydrogen-bonded anti structures. Conformer 5 has the shortest H···N distance, about 2.17 Å, but its terminal-chain dihedral is near 90 degrees rather than a staggered anti or gauche minimum, so torsional strain offsets much of the hydrogen-bond benefit. Conformers 6 and 30 have the same general compromise, with intermediate approximately 90–100 degree chain torsions and weaker contacts than 5. Third, conformers 26, 25, 2, 27, 8, and 24 are open O/N rotamers with O···N near 3.68 Å. They lose the intramolecular hydrogen bond but retain extended, mostly staggered chains and avoid close heteroatom repulsion. Conformers 26 and 25 are preferred within this group because the hydroxymethyl substituent is arranged more cleanly opposite the incoming chain; 8 and 24 place both large central substituents more gauche to the chain and are somewhat more crowded. Conformer 21 is the better of the open, terminal-chain-gauche structures because its hydroxymethyl group is anti to the nearby chain segment; 19 is more crowded around the central carbon. Finally, conformers 1, 3, 17, 11, 28, 13, 4, and 20 bring O moderately close to N but direct H toward the wrong side of the pyramidal amine, giving O–H···N angles only around 98–102 degrees and poor lone-pair alignment. Thus they receive little hydrogen-bond stabilization while retaining close O/N or hydroxyl/ring contacts. The extended-chain members 1, 3, and 17 are less unfavorable than the corresponding chain-gauche members. Among the last group, 20 has an especially unproductive hydroxyl direction and a roughly 2.5 Å H-to-ring-carbon approach, while 4 also has a relatively short nonproductive O/N contact. Differences within the 14–25 and 26–30 ranges are especially uncertain because dispersion and small torsional-energy differences cannot be quantified reliably from XYZ geometry alone.

1. The molecule is acyclic, and all conformers retain a normal tetrahedral central carbon and approximately planar amide; there is no gross bond-angle strain or unphysical atomic overlap. The main differences are rotation of the ethylamino and amide groups, weak five-membered intramolecular hydrogen-bond motifs, and gauche crowding of the ethyl group. 2. Conformer 29 has the best overall compromise: an extended, anti-like ethyl arrangement (terminal methyl–central carbon separation about 3.76 Å), an amino N–H···O=C contact of about 2.20 Å and 111°, and an amide N–H···N≡C contact near 2.76 Å and 123°. Conformers 14 and 18 have slightly stronger N–H···O contacts (about 2.17/113° and 2.15/114°) plus weak nitrile contacts, but their ethyl groups are more gauche; 18 is slightly more crowded than 14, with a methyl–central carbon separation near 3.04 Å versus 3.15 Å. 3. Conformers 30, 7, and 25 combine extended ethyl geometries with short amide N–H···amine-N contacts. The approximate H···N distances/angles are 2.11 Å/110° for 30, 2.12 Å/109° for 7, and 2.16 Å/107° for 25. These contacts are angularly constrained but involve a more basic acceptor than the nitrile. 4. Conformers 23 and 17 have extended ethyl groups and moderately directed amide N–H···nitrile contacts near 2.73–2.74 Å and 122–123°. Conformer 9 has the best-oriented nitrile contact of the set, about 2.37 Å and 130°, but pays a gauche penalty because its terminal methyl lies only about 3.12 Å from the central carbon. 5. Conformer 26 has two weaker contacts—N–H···O around 2.29 Å/108° and N–H···N≡C around 2.72 Å/122°—but is folded. Conformers 20 and 22 mainly benefit from amino N–H···O=C contacts near 2.22 Å/108° and 2.19 Å/110°; 20 is less tightly folded. Conformer 24 has a weaker, more bent O contact near 2.30 Å/104°, but its extended ethyl group partly compensates. 6. Conformers 19 and 27 have short amide-H···amine-N distances near 2.11 Å and angles near 109°, but both are gauche. Conformer 21 has a moderate nitrile contact near 2.73 Å/121°, while its possible amino-H···O contact is poorly aligned. Conformers 1 and 3 are relatively open and extended but have only weak contacts; 13, 6, 15, and 4 represent progressively less favorable compromises between weak hydrogen bonding and ethyl crowding. 7. Conformer 8 is extended but places the amine and carbonyl oxygen close without directing the N–H toward oxygen (H···O about 2.50 Å and only about 95°), so the proximity gives little stabilization. Conformers 28, 11, and 5 have weak, bent amide-H···amine contacts and varying gauche strain. Conformers 12 and 16 have only long or poorly aligned nitrile/oxygen contacts, while 10 combines a tight gauche ethyl geometry with a poorly directed amide-H···amine contact. Conformer 2 has neither a useful donor–acceptor alignment nor an extended ethyl arrangement and is therefore placed last. 8. The ordering is most uncertain within the middle and lower groups because all putative intramolecular hydrogen bonds are geometrically constrained and relatively weak; differences among adjacent entries should not be interpreted as large energy gaps.

The molecule is acyclic, so ring strain is absent and no conformer shows a catastrophic nonbonded clash. The main geometric discriminator is the orientation of NH2 relative to the ester oxygens. Conformers 2, 5, 6, 20, 21, and 23 have the clearest N–H···O=C contact: H···O is about 2.35–2.36 Å with N–H···O angles near 125°, making this the most favorable family. Within it, 23 has the most nearly extended ethoxy C–C–O–C arrangement; 6 is also relatively extended, while 20 and 21 have a more gauche/folded ethoxy arm, with 21 having the slightly better hydrogen-bond geometry. Conformers 7, 12, 14, 18, 25, and 28 instead direct an N–H toward the ester single-bond oxygen. Their best H···O distances are approximately 2.35 Å for 7, 12, 25, and 28, but this oxygen is a weaker acceptor than the carbonyl oxygen. Conformers 28 and 12 also have extended ethoxy geometries and are therefore preferred within this family; the contacts in 18 and especially 14 are longer, about 2.47–2.50 Å. Conformers 1, 3, 17, 26, 29, and 30 place N near the carbonyl oxygen but orient the hydrogens less effectively: the best H···O distances are generally about 2.60–2.63 Å with angles around 110–115°. Extended ethoxy arrangements favor 26, 17, 29, and 30 over the more folded 1 and 3. The remaining conformers place N near the alkoxy oxygen but have only moderate donor alignment, usually H···O about 2.48–2.53 Å. Among these, 8, 24, 10, 4, 27, 15, and 9 have the less strained, more extended ethoxy arm, whereas 11, 13, 16, 19, and 22 are gauche/folded and are placed last. No decisive secondary long-range contact separates many members of the same family, so ordering within the close groups—and especially the boundary between strong alkoxy hydrogen bonding and weak carbonyl hydrogen bonding—is uncertain.

1. The molecule is an acyclic propargyl ether bearing a secondary alcohol, so there is no ring strain. None of the structures has an obvious catastrophic nonbonded clash; the ranking is therefore controlled mainly by backbone torsions, the O–C–C–O arrangement, methyl/ether gauche interactions, and possible intramolecular OH···O(ether) attraction. 2. Conformers 3, 18, 19, and 28 combine an extended C4–O–C6–C7 segment (C4···C7 about 3.68 Å), an approximately anti ether-to-methyl arrangement (Oether···Cmethyl about 3.7 Å), and a close hydroxyl-H···Oether contact near 2.29 Å. These are the best-balanced structures and are nearly degenerate; their internal hydrogen-bond geometry is bent, so its stabilization should not be overestimated. 3. Conformer 11 is uniquely extended across both principal backbone torsions (C3···C6 about 3.62 Å and C4···C7 about 3.68 Å) and retains an OH···Oether contact, but it places the methyl group gauche to the ether oxygen, putting it just below the leading set. Conformers 27, 14, and 16 also have the extended C4–O–C6–C7 backbone and close donor/acceptor geometry, but likewise carry the less favorable methyl-gauche arrangement. 4. Conformers 24, 13, and 2 have especially short H···Oether contacts near 2.20 Å and an anti ether-to-methyl relationship, but a gauche/nonideal backbone segment (C4···C7 around 3.13 Å) offsets that benefit. Conformer 26 has similar attraction but a more distorted roughly 80–90 degree backbone torsion, and 7 distorts two backbone torsions to maintain the contact, so these are progressively lower. 5. Conformers 5, 8, and 21 lack a useful hydrogen bond, but retain a favorable anti methyl relationship and keep the two oxygens farther apart, near 3.1 Å, avoiding the unfavorable close O···O geometry seen when the OH points away. Conformers 22, 29, 10, and 9 have an extended backbone and well-separated oxygens (about 3.6 Å), but the hydroxyl is anti while the larger methyl group is gauche to the ether oxygen. 6. In 25, 17, and 30 the oxygens are close, about 2.78 Å, but the hydroxyl hydrogen is not directed toward the ether oxygen (H···O about 2.8 Å), giving little hydrogen-bond compensation for the close oxygen contact. Conformer 20 separates the oxygens somewhat better but has two nonideal backbone torsions. 7. Conformers 23, 6, and 4 have no useful OH···O contact and combine multiple gauche relationships with the methyl-gauche arrangement. Conformers 15, 12, and 1 add more distorted backbone geometries or unfavorable dipole/contact orientations and form the least favorable tier. The order within the near-degenerate groups—especially 3/28/19/18, 27/14/16, 24/13/2, and 22/29/10/9—is uncertain without electronic-structure or force-field energies.

The connectivity is a substituted vicinal diol: one OH is on the cyclopropane-bearing carbon and the other on the adjacent isopropyl-substituted carbon. The cyclopropane geometry is very similar throughout, with no exceptional bond distortion, so the main discriminants are the O–C–C–O torsion, OH orientation, and 1,4 O···C contacts. Conformer 6 has the best intramolecular OH···O arrangement: O···O is about 2.66 Å and the donor hydrogen is the most favorably directed of the set, while the carbon skeleton remains reasonably open. Conformers 14 and 25 have similarly compact O···O separations near 2.73 Å and useful, though bent, hydrogen bonds; 14 has slightly less crowding around the isopropyl methyls. Conformer 17 also has a short O···O distance near 2.70 Å but a less linear donor geometry. Conformers 21, 5, and 18 retain weak five-membered intramolecular hydrogen bonds with O···O around 2.77–2.83 Å and no severe heavy-atom contact. Conformers 3 and 30 have longer and more bent OH···O contacts, so their stabilization is smaller. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded, O–C–C–O-extended structures, 28 and 29 are especially balanced: the hydroxyl bond vectors are approximately opposed and the principal O···C contacts are around or above 3.1 Å. Conformers 1, 7, and 23 are comparably open and are close in energy to that pair. Conformers 26, 11, and 27 have only weak, bent OH···O contacts but remain preferable to more crowded extended rotamers; 8 is a relatively favorable extended structure with opposed OH orientations. Conformer 2 is penalized by an approximately 2.87 Å isopropyl-carbon···O contact despite its weak OH···O approach. The remaining extended conformers progressively introduce shorter 1,4 O···C contacts: 22 is moderate; 16 has one contact near 2.83 Å; 13, 19, 12, and 15 have combinations near 2.85–3.0 Å. Conformers 20, 9, and 4 place the oxygens on the same side without a well-directed hydrogen bond; 4 is particularly compact at O···O about 2.73 Å. Conformers 24 and 10 are placed last because they combine poor hydrogen-bond geometry with the tightest heavy-atom contacts, approximately 2.79 Å in 24 and two contacts near 2.85 Å in 10. The middle and lower portions are uncertain because many structures differ mainly by OH torsion or exchange of symmetry-related methyl/cyclopropyl groups, so several adjacent entries should be regarded as near-ties.

All structures have essentially the same aziridine geometry and bond lengths, so differential ring strain is small. There are no hydrogen-bond donors; the main distinctions are rotations about C–C, C–N, and C–O bonds, steric gauche contacts, and repulsion/dipole alignment between the tertiary aziridine N and ether O. First, conformers 2, 4, and 15 place N and O well apart (N···O about 3.6–3.7 Å) while also keeping the terminal O-methyl group approximately anti to the backbone; they have the cleanest overall staggered geometries. Conformer 2 is placed first because its ethyl terminus is anti to the aziridine substituent and its remaining heavy-atom contacts are balanced near or above 3.15 Å. Conformer 4 has slightly cleaner ring-to-side-chain clearance than 15; in 15 one aziridine-carbon/methoxymethyl contact is close to 3.0 Å. Next, 24, 20, 30, and 10 also have long N···O distances near 3.68 Å and well-balanced aziridine/side-chain separation, but their C–C–O–Me arrangements are gauche, with the O-methyl carbon only about 3.1 Å from the central backbone carbon. Their ordering is therefore subtle. Conformers 9 and 16 retain the favorable anti N/O arrangement but have an additional gauche ethyl orientation; 25 instead keeps the ether methyl anti but places the ethyl methyl gauche to both major central substituents. Conformer 3 has favorable terminal anti arrangements, but N···O is only about 3.03 Å, so it follows the best N/O-anti structures. Conformers 28, 6, and 12 similarly have anti O-methyl geometries but gauche N–C–C–O arrangements; 28 has the largest N···O distance of this subgroup (about 3.11 Å), while 6 and 12 are near 3.02–3.04 Å. Conformer 18 is unusual: both N···O and ethyl-carbon···O separations are relatively long (about 3.54 and 3.48 Å), but this is achieved by a skewed, less ideally staggered backbone torsion and a gauche ether methyl, making its placement uncertain. Conformers 17, 27, and 23 have comparable gauche N/O geometries but otherwise balanced contacts; 17 has the best O-methyl clearance, followed by 27 and 23. Conformer 7 benefits from anti N/O placement but has both an unfavorable ethyl orientation and gauche ether methyl. Conformer 8 has a short N···O distance near 2.94 Å and an additional relatively close N···O-methyl approach. Conformers 26 and 13 have N···O near 3.1–3.16 Å plus gauche ethyl and ether arrangements. Conformer 19 removes the ether-methyl gauche penalty but leaves the ethyl methyl gauche to both central substituents. Conformer 21 has the shortest N···O distance, about 2.91 Å, together with an O-methyl/N approach near 3.27 Å. The final group has multiple simultaneous close contacts: 5, 14, 22, and 11 place O gauche to both N and the ethyl side, with ethyl-carbon···O around 2.9–3.1 Å; 11 additionally has the least favorable ethyl orientation and is therefore last. Conformers 29 and 1 avoid the double heteroatom/ethyl contact but retain several gauche interactions and thus remain low. Differences within the middle clusters are likely only a few tenths of a kcal/mol and are correspondingly uncertain without an electronic-structure calculation.

The molecule is an acyclic diol, HOCH2–CH2–CH(CH3)–CH(OH)–CH2–CH3. The dominant stabilizing motif is a six-membered pseudo-ring formed by an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond; its benefit must be balanced against gauche and near-eclipsed backbone torsions. No structure has a severe nonbonded atomic clash, so the ordering is mainly hydrogen bonding plus torsional strain.

The best geometries are 26 and 16. Both have short, nearly linear primary-OH-to-secondary-O hydrogen bonds: O···O is about 2.74 Å and H···O is about 1.82 and 1.86 Å, respectively. Their ethyl and branched-backbone substituents also retain favorable anti relationships, giving relatively chair-like pseudo-rings. Conformers 29 and 14 have similarly short O···O contacts of 2.73–2.74 Å and H···O contacts of 1.82–1.85 Å, but each introduces a gauche terminal-ethyl torsion. Conformer 1 preserves favorable heavy-atom anti relationships, although its hydrogen bond is longer and more bent (H···O about 1.97 Å), placing it below those four.

Conformers 21, 10, and 28 retain good hydrogen bonds while accepting additional gauche strain. Conformer 21 has one of the shortest H···O distances, about 1.81 Å, but its compact backbone has unfavorable gauche relationships around both central bonds. Conformer 10 has a somewhat weaker 1.92 Å hydrogen bond but fewer unfavorable central arrangements. Conformer 28 has a strong 1.85 Å contact but more large-group gauche crowding. Conformer 7 has a good 1.85 Å hydrogen bond and otherwise favorable pseudo-ring substitution, but the terminal ethyl torsion is near 100 degrees rather than staggered, producing appreciable eclipsing strain.

Conformers 30, 8, 22, 24, 15, and 17 are progressively more crowded hydrogen-bonded structures. Their H···O distances range from roughly 1.82 to 1.96 Å, but they contain combinations of ethyl/backbone gauche interactions and cases where both large substituents around the CH–CH2 bond are gauche to the terminal CH2OH group. Conformer 8 has a relatively long hydrogen bond but a favorable anti relationship across the central C–C bond. Conformers 22 and 24 have stronger hydrogen bonds but an additional gauche ethyl torsion. Conformers 15 and 17 use the secondary alcohol as donor and have slightly weaker or more strained arrangements.

Conformers 19, 3, and 2 do form recognizable hydrogen bonds, with H···O distances near 1.95, 1.98, and 1.92 Å, respectively. However, the central C–C torsion is close to 90–100 degrees, creating eclipsing strain between large backbone fragments. Conformer 2 adds another gauche ethyl torsion, making it the least favorable of the clearly hydrogen-bonded set.

Among the open structures, 25 is best: the three principal carbon-chain torsions are anti, and the two hydroxyl-group dipoles are approximately opposed, although the oxygens are too far apart for hydrogen bonding. Conformer 27 is also largely all-anti and has favorable overall dipole opposition; 13 and 11 are similarly extended but have less favorable hydroxyl dipole arrangements. Conformers 18 and 23 each introduce one ethyl gauche torsion. Conformer 6 has two gauche relationships but gains a weak, bent O–H···O contact with H···O about 2.27 Å. Conformer 4 has a folded CH–CH2 torsion without a useful hydrogen bond. Conformers 20 and 5 contain near-eclipsed torsions, while 12 combines a gauche torsion with a strongly distorted central torsion. Conformer 9 has two substantially nonstaggered backbone regions and, despite an O···O distance near 2.9 Å, both O–H vectors point poorly for hydrogen bonding.

The largest uncertainty is among neighboring compact hydrogen-bonded structures, especially 21 versus 10, 30 versus 8, and 22 versus 24, because hydrogen-bond strength and gauche penalties are comparable. The open all-anti structures may also interchange depending on the electronic-structure method and treatment of intramolecular electrostatics.

All structures retain essentially the same cyclopropane geometry, so differential ring strain is small; the ranking is controlled mainly by side-chain torsions, intramolecular O–H···O=C contacts, and secondarily by O···O or methyl/ring crowding. Conformers 9 and 4 have the best hydrogen bonds from the ring alcohol to the carbonyl: H···O is about 1.87 Å, O···O about 2.80 Å, and the O–H···O angle about 157°, with 9 having marginally less secondary carbonyl-O/ring crowding. Conformer 18 has nearly the same linear geometry but a slightly longer H···O distance near 1.91 Å. Conformers 8 and 20 also form clear ring-OH···carbonyl contacts, but their angles are closer to 149–150° and H···O distances about 1.95–1.96 Å. Conformer 26 instead uses the alcohol attached to the substituted cyclopropane carbon; its approximately 1.97 Å contact is more bent, but still competitive. Conformer 3 has a roughly 2.02 Å, 141° contact and is therefore somewhat weaker. Conformers 19, 22, and 23 have recognizable but substantially bent alcohol-to-carbonyl hydrogen bonds, with H···O near 2.05–2.07 Å and angles near 131–132°; 19 is slightly better aligned, while 22 and 23 are nearly degenerate. Conformer 29 has a still weaker, more bent contact near 2.14 Å. Conformers 12, 27, and 30 only have long and bent approaches to the carbonyl, so their hydrogen-bond stabilization should be modest; 12 and 27 have shorter H···O distances than 30. Conformer 13 has an approximately 2.47 Å approach but poor angular alignment, placing it at the boundary between weakly bound and open conformers. Among structures without useful hydrogen bonding, 15, 6, and 24 keep the carbonyl and both alcohol oxygens relatively separated and avoid obvious nonbonded compression. Conformers 10 and 5 have only very weak, long carbonyl approaches but otherwise reasonable torsions. Conformers 17, 7, 25, and 16 are broadly unstrained open arrangements, with small ordering differences based on compactness and oxygen separation. Conformers 14, 11, 21, 1, and 2 place the carbonyl or methyl group progressively closer to the oxygen-rich ring region without gaining a properly directed hydrogen bond. Conformer 28 is least favored because the carbonyl and ring-alcohol oxygens approach to roughly 2.96 Å while the O–H vector is poorly directed, producing more O···O crowding than hydrogen-bond stabilization. The top hydrogen-bonded groups are reasonably distinguishable, but the ordering among the non-hydrogen-bonded conformers, and especially the near ties 9/4 and 22/23, is uncertain without electronic energies.

The molecule is acyclic, so the main geometric discriminants are intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bonding, staggered versus double-gauche placement about the C–C backbone, orientation of the two carbonyl dipoles, and whether the ketone methyl points toward the hydroxy-bearing carbon. Conformer 17 has the best hydrogen bond: H···O(ketone) is about 1.92 Å with an O–H···O angle near 138°, while the terminal methyl is anti to the bulkier ketone branch and the carbonyls remain well separated. Conformers 4, 15, and 10 form the next strongest contacts. For 4 and 10 the acceptor is the ketone oxygen (about 2.01–2.05 Å and 130–131°); 4 has the better backbone anti placement. Conformer 15 has a similarly strong, more linear contact to the aldehyde oxygen (about 2.01 Å, 137°) and favorable opposing carbonyl orientation, but the aldehyde is the weaker acceptor and the ketone methyl is somewhat closer to the hydroxy-bearing center. Conformers 22, 18, and 29 have weaker ketone-directed contacts, with H···O about 2.10–2.19 Å and angles around 123–125°. Of these, 22 has particularly favorable carbonyl and methyl placement; 18 has the shortest contact; 29 has less favorable carbonyl-dipole alignment. Conformers 5 and 23 have moderately bent aldehyde-directed contacts (roughly 2.18–2.24 Å and 129–131°), but both pay additional gauche penalties. Conformers 24, 14, and 21 retain weaker aldehyde-directed contacts near 2.2 Å; 24 benefits from widely separated, opposing carbonyl oxygens, whereas 14 and 21 have less favorable backbone packing. Among structures without a credible O–H···O contact, 3 and 16 are favored because the terminal methyl is anti to the ketone branch, the ketone methyl points away from the hydroxy-bearing carbon, and the carbonyl arrangement avoids a strong same-direction dipole interaction. Conformers 30, 25, and 27 also have good anti backbone and carbonyl arrangements, although their ketone methyl is more syn/gauche to the backbone. Conformers 11 and 8 have favorable carbonyl opposition and an outward ketone methyl but place the terminal methyl gauche to both carbonyl branches. Conformers 26 and 9 are relatively open but keep the terminal methyl anti to the smaller aldehyde rather than the ketone. The remaining open conformers have progressively less favorable combinations of double-gauche packing, ketone-methyl proximity, or carbonyl dipole alignment. In particular, 12 and 19 bring the carbonyl oxygens relatively close (about 3.4–3.5 Å) with poorly compensating dipoles, while 13, 28, 2, and especially 20 have less favorable end-to-end/outward carbonyl arrangements combined with anti placement toward the smaller branch or ketone-methyl crowding. No severe nonbonded clash is present, so positions outside the strong-hydrogen-bond tier are uncertain and could readily interchange after electronic-structure optimization; the middle and lower ordering should be regarded as qualitative.

1. The common skeleton is a planar aromatic pyrrole bearing ethyl and hydroxymethyl groups at the two alpha carbons. The ring geometries are essentially identical, so ring strain is not a useful discriminator; the ranking is governed mainly by the two benzylic torsions and their ortho contacts. 2. The most favorable structures place both the ethyl methyl carbon and the hydroxymethyl oxygen out of the pyrrole plane. Conformers 7, 19, 21, 3, 6, 13, 5, 11, and 27 have this pattern. Within this group, 7 gives the best-balanced clearance of O from both pyrrolic N and the neighboring ring carbon (about 3.3 Å each); 19, 21, 3, 6, and 13 are similarly open. In 5, 11, and especially 27, O leans progressively closer to the carbon/H on the opposite ortho side, so they are placed slightly lower. These differences are small. 3. Conformers 8, 16, and 18 retain the favorable out-of-plane ethyl group, but O leans toward N, with N...O near 3.04 Å. This is only marginally shorter than the N/O van der Waals sum, but it is less favorable than the balanced top group. There is no convincing hydrogen bond: the pyrrolic N is not an acceptor, and the N-H...O geometry is markedly bent. Conformer 18 has the closest O approach to the N-H region and is therefore last in this subgroup. 4. In 14, 10, 4, and 15 the ethyl group remains out of plane, while O is approximately in the ring plane on the carbon-H side. N...O is long (about 3.7 Å), but O approaches the neighboring ring carbon/H more closely, around 3.0/2.9 Å. The OH hydrogen is also somewhat closer to that ring H in 4 and 15, placing them after 14 and 10. 5. Conformers 28, 29, 17, and 2 have a good out-of-plane hydroxymethyl orientation but an in-plane ethyl methyl group. The terminal methyl carbon lies only roughly 2.9-3.0 Å from the neighboring ring H region, producing more steric crowding than the out-of-plane ethyl arrangements. Conformer 28 has the largest clearance and is preferred within this set. 6. Conformers 23, 24, and 26 combine that in-plane ethyl penalty with an O orientation leaning toward N; 23 has slightly better methyl-side clearance. Conformers 12 and 20 keep ethyl out of plane but place O in-plane toward N, giving N...O about 2.70 Å and H(N)...O about 2.40 Å. The N-H...O angle is near 96 degrees rather than linear, so this is treated as a close-contact penalty rather than a stabilizing hydrogen bond. 7. Conformers 30, 9, 22, and 1 place both terminal heavy groups in relatively crowded in-plane orientations, accumulating contacts on both ortho sides; 30 and 9 have slightly better methyl clearance. Conformer 25 is least favorable because its in-plane methyl points toward the pyrrolic N-H side: C(methyl)...N is about 2.87 Å and one methyl-H/N-H separation is approximately 1.9 Å, while its oxygen also leans toward N. 8. Many neighboring entries, especially within the first nine and within symmetry-related pairs such as 8/16 and 12/20, are effectively near-degenerate. Dispersion and the very shallow ethyl/hydroxymethyl torsional potentials could readily swap adjacent positions.

The molecule is acyclic, with a tertiary alcohol center bearing methyl, CH2CHO, and CH2CCH substituents, so the main energetic variables are the O–H orientation and rotations of the aldehyde and ethynyl-containing arms. First, six geometries contain a clear five-membered intramolecular O–H···O=C contact. Conformer 1 has the strongest geometry, with H···O about 1.94 Å and an O–H···O angle near 141°, although its two carbon arms are relatively compact. Conformer 16 has a 2.07 Å, approximately 132° contact and a favorable aldehyde/propargyl anti arrangement. Conformer 21 has a somewhat weaker 2.12 Å, approximately 128° hydrogen bond but the best overall staggering: the aldehyde and ethynyl substituents are placed anti to the largest opposing groups. Conformers 26 and 6 retain hydrogen bonds near 2.15 and 2.11 Å, respectively; 26 benefits from a better ethynyl-arm arrangement, while 6 has the slightly better hydrogen-bond geometry. Conformer 2 has a respectable 2.08 Å, approximately 132° contact but leaves both carbon arms in less favorable gauche combinations, making it the least favorable of the hydrogen-bonded set. Second, among non-hydrogen-bonded structures, conformer 11 has the best combination of staggered torsions: the aldehyde carbon is anti to the propargyl arm, the ethynyl group is anti to the aldehyde arm, and the hydroxyl hydrogen is directed away from the bulky substituents. Conformers 24 and 4 each preserve one of these especially favorable anti relationships and orient O–H away from CH2CHO; conformer 7 has good carbon-arm staggering but a less favorable hydroxyl orientation. Conformers 10 and 5 also keep the aldehyde anti to the propargyl arm, with 10 having the better O–H orientation. Conformers 14 and 13 are more compact; 13 is additionally penalized because the two oxygen atoms approach to about 3.53 Å while the hydroxyl hydrogen points away, giving acceptor–acceptor proximity without hydrogen-bond compensation. Third, conformers 23, 12, 9, and 30 keep the ethynyl group anti to the aldehyde arm but place the aldehyde anti to oxygen rather than to a carbon substituent. The more extended 23 and 12 geometries are preferred over 9 and 30, where the carbonyl oxygen approaches the methyl region more closely. Conformer 15 has favorable aldehyde-arm staggering but an unfavorable ethynyl and hydroxyl orientation. Conformer 28 is moderately staggered but compact, including an O=C···C(alkyne) separation around 3.4 Å. Conformers 29, 27, and 25 each contain one relatively unfavorable carbon-arm torsion; 27 also folds the carbonyl oxygen toward the alkyne at roughly 3.4 Å, while 25 brings the carbonyl oxygen near the methyl group. Finally, conformers 8, 22, 17, and 19 combine an aldehyde orientation gauche to both carbon substituents with a hydroxyl hydrogen directed toward the less bulky methyl side; 19 has the closest carbonyl-oxygen/methyl approach of this subgroup. Conformer 3 has somewhat better carbon-arm staggering but an uncompensated O···O approach near 3.42 Å. Conformers 18 and 20 place both major arms in the least favorable torsional classes; 20 is placed last because it also brings the carbonyl oxygen to roughly 3.2 Å from the methyl carbon. No geometry shows an unmistakable sub-van-der-Waals heavy-atom clash, so ordering within the non-hydrogen-bonded middle and lower groups is substantially more uncertain than separation of the hydrogen-bonded set.

All structures retain normal tetrahydrofuran-like bond geometry, so the main distinctions are intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bonding, side-chain torsions, and secondary methyl/side-chain crowding rather than gross ring strain. Conformers 29, 28, and 11 have the best combined geometry: ring-O···H distances of about 1.98–2.00 Å, O···O distances near 2.79–2.81 Å, and O–H···O angles near 139–140 degrees. Their hydroxyalkyl groups are also directed away from the bulky ring-carbon/methyl side, making 29/28/11 the leading near-degenerate group. Conformer 14 has a similarly strong approximately 1.98 Å contact and approximately 139 degree angle, but its folded side-chain torsion places the terminal carbon closer to the substituted ring carbon, so it follows that group. Conformers 23 and 8 also form O–H···O contacts, but the angles are more bent, approximately 129 and 134 degrees, respectively; 8 additionally has the closest approach of the folded side chain toward the methyl region, making it the weaker of these two. Conformer 13 has only a weak, bent contact: H···O is about 2.58 Å and O–H···O about 119 degrees, but this still gives some stabilization while retaining a favorable side-chain orientation. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 1, 3, 9, 6, 26, 18, 17, and 7 place the terminal hydroxyalkyl carbon roughly anti to the bulkier substituted ring-carbon direction and show no important short contacts; their ordering is consequently sensitive to small ring-puckering, torsional, and dipole differences. Conformer 4 has a very weak long-range O–H···O approach, while 24 and 22 bring the two oxygen-bearing portions moderately close without directing the hydroxyl hydrogen effectively toward the ring oxygen, making that folding less favorable. Conformers 12, 16, 20, 2, and 27 use the alternative staggered side-chain family; they avoid direct clashes but place the terminal carbon gauche to the bulkier ring-carbon direction and lack hydrogen-bond compensation. The final group, 30, 19, 25, 5, 10, 15, and 21, combines that less favorable torsional family with progressively greater proximity to the methyl/substituted-ring region. In particular, 15 and 21 have terminal-carbon to substituted-ring-carbon separations near 3.3 Å together with relatively compact methyl-side geometries. No conformer has a catastrophic steric clash, so positions within the non-hydrogen-bonded middle and lower groups are substantially more uncertain than the hydrogen-bond-based separation at the top.

The molecule has three important rotatable regions: the central C–C bond between the substituted methine and CH2O group, the methine–aldehyde bond, and the CH2–O bond. I first favored staggered geometries placing the larger methyl/formyl/CH2O groups approximately anti, then checked whether folding introduced short heteroatom contacts. Conformers 16 and 20 are the cleanest extended arrangements: the carbonyl and imidate ends remain well separated, O(carbonyl)···O(ether) is about 4.1 Å, O(carbonyl)···N is about 5.9 Å, and the major substituents occupy favorable anti-like positions. Conformers 7 and 10 retain similarly favorable central and aldehyde orientations but have a less favorable terminal CH2–O rotamer. Conformers 25, 26, 28, 11, 8, 18, 6, and 5 remain mostly staggered and clash-free, although they introduce one or more gauche relationships; 6 additionally has a relatively close O···O contact near 3.16 Å, while 5 brings N toward the carbonyl region to roughly 2.8 Å. Conformers 17, 23, 12, 19, 13, 30, 1, and 29 are still chemically reasonable but place a larger substituent gauche where an anti arrangement is available or produce less favorable carbonyl/imine dipole proximity. Conformers 27, 2, 9, 22, 14, and 21 accumulate two unfavorable torsional choices, often leaving the ether substituent anti to the small methine H rather than to methyl or formyl. The clearest high-energy geometries are 4, 24, 15, and 3: each folds the imine N onto the aldehyde carbon, with N···C(carbonyl) only about 2.10–2.13 Å and O(carbonyl)···N about 2.64–2.68 Å. Although the approximately 101–105 degree approach is reminiscent of an n→π* or incipient nucleophilic-attack geometry, at such a short distance and without bond formation or proton transfer it is treated primarily as a severe nonbonded compression. The nominally short N–H···O contacts in 24 and 15 are not compensating hydrogen bonds: H···O is about 2.82–2.83 Å but the N–H···O angle is only about 69 degrees. Ordering within the broad middle group is uncertain because torsional, dipolar, and weak dispersion differences are small and no electronic energies are supplied.

The six-membered ring is formed by carbons 5-10 in each block, with a short C6-C7 distance of about 1.32 Å identifying a cyclohexene rather than a saturated cyclohexane. Consequently, the lowest-strain structures should have the usual half-chair geometry: the four-carbon allylic/alkenic segment is nearly planar, while the two saturated ring atoms pucker in a staggered fashion. Conformers 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 18, 20, 21, 24, and 28 best preserve this geometry; their substituted allylic-to-opposite-ring-carbon separation is close to 3.0 Å and they avoid serious transannular compression. Within this group, 1, 21, 24, 4, 18, and 8 place the CH2OH oxygen relatively far outside the ring envelope, generally about 3.0 Å or more from the nearest nonbonded ring carbon, with little steric crowding. Conformers 3, 13, and 9 also point O-H outward and are close in energy, although their oxygen approaches one ring carbon slightly more closely, around 2.9-2.95 Å. Conformers 2, 11, and 12 remain low-strain but have less favorable tangential or partially inward O-H orientations. In 28 and 14 the hydroxyl hydrogen points more toward the ring cavity, and 10 and especially 20 have the least favorable inward hydroxyl orientation in this low-strain ring family; in 20 the oxygen also approaches a nonbonded ring carbon at roughly 2.82 Å. A second family—27, 15, 19, 30, 29, 6, 22, 16, 23, and 7—has a more compressed half-chair, with the corresponding across-ring separation around 2.74-2.79 Å. These are assigned a moderate strain penalty. Conformers 27 and 15 have comparatively clear external side-chain arrangements, followed by 19 and 30; 29 and 6 have outward O-H bonds but somewhat tighter oxygen-ring approaches. Conformers 16, 23, and 7 direct O-H noticeably back toward the ring and are placed near the bottom of this family. Conformers 5, 26, and 17 have more boat/twist-like ring geometries, with the three across-ring distances becoming unusually similar near 2.9 Å rather than showing the normal cyclohexene half-chair pattern; 5 is least unfavorable because its hydroxyl points outward, while 26 and 17 combine this ring penalty with inward hydroxyl orientations. Conformer 25 is the clearest high-strain outlier: one pair of nominally opposite ring carbons is only about 2.34 Å apart, indicating strong boat-like/transannular compression despite acceptable external substituent directions. There is only one oxygen atom, so none of the conformers can form a conventional intramolecular donor-acceptor hydrogen bond; hydroxyl orientation therefore enters mainly through steric and dipolar effects. The ordering within each half-chair family is uncertain because many differences are only small CH2OH and O-H torsional changes, but the separation between normal half-chairs, compressed half-chairs, boat/twist forms, and the severely compressed conformer 25 is more robust.

The molecule is an acyclic N-formyl amino alcohol, so the principal geometric discriminator is intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the terminal alcohol and the formamide, followed by the gauche/anti pattern of the flexible carbon chain. First, conformers 3, 4, 7, 8, 11, 17, 20, 24, 28, and 29 contain an O-H···O=C contact. The best examples have H···O distances near 1.88-1.99 Å and nearly linear donor geometry: 29 has about 1.92 Å with an almost linear O-H···O arrangement; 20 has about 1.88 Å and approximately 162 degrees; 24 has about 1.92 Å and approximately 166 degrees; and 7 has about 1.90 Å and approximately 158 degrees. Conformers 17 and 4 are exceptionally linear but have slightly longer O···O separations near 2.95-2.96 Å. Conformer 28 remains a good hydrogen-bonded structure but is more bent, while 11 and 8 have the longest H···O distances, about 2.11 and 2.09 Å, and angles near 146 degrees. Second, conformers 5, 9, 14, 16, 19, 25, and 27 contain N-H···O(alcohol) contacts that close a favorable six-heavy-atom pseudoring. The strongest are 5 and 14, with H···O near 1.91-1.93 Å and N-H···O angles around 144-148 degrees. Conformer 9 is similarly short but has less favorable alkyl torsions. Conformers 16 and 27 have approximately 2.02 Å contacts, whereas 19 and 25 are appreciably bent, with about 2.17 Å H···O distances and angles near 128-130 degrees. Conformer 18 has only a weak, bent N-H···O approach, roughly 2.46 Å and 116 degrees. Third, torsional strain differentiates structures with similar hydrogen bonds. Conformer 29 combines its strong O-H···O=C bond with an extended C5-C6-C7-N segment and relatively separated nonbonded substituents, making it the best overall compromise. Conformers 20, 24, and 7 also combine short hydrogen bonds with comparatively open methyl/hydroxymethyl arrangements. Conformers 17 and 4 retain an anti-like backbone but each introduces additional gauche contacts; 28 is less linear at the hydrogen bond; and 3 has an excellent hydrogen bond but several approximately 3.0 Å gauche endpoint contacts around the stereogenic carbon. The strong six-membered N-H···O motifs in 5 and 14 therefore compete with the more torsionally crowded O-H···O=C structures. Fourth, among structures lacking a convincing hydrogen bond, 30 is favored because its main C5-C6-C7-N segment is the most extended. Conformers 15, 1, 26, and 23 have reasonably separated substituents but retain a gauche backbone. Structures 10, 13, and 2 have similar non-hydrogen-bonded torsional patterns, while 21, 6, 22, and 12 accumulate less favorable gauche or poorly separated terminal-group arrangements. No unmistakable severe atomic overlap is present, so the middle and especially the non-hydrogen-bonded tail are uncertain; small changes from dispersion, solvent, zero-point energy, or electronic-structure treatment could reorder neighboring entries.

1. All conformers retain essentially the same aziridine geometry and normal bond lengths, so the main discriminator is side-chain torsion and intramolecular hydrogen bonding rather than differential ring strain. 2. Conformer 23 has the best distinct interaction: a favorable six-membered O–H···N closure, with H···N about 2.13 Å, O···N about 2.80 Å, and an approximately 147° donor–H–acceptor angle. The aziridine nitrogen is a stronger acceptor than an alcohol oxygen, placing 23 first. 3. A large group forms a five-membered O–H···O closure between the primary and secondary alcohols. The strongest geometries occur in 3, 17, 14, 16, 12, 9, 24, 21, 13, and 29: their H···O distances are roughly 1.92–2.01 Å and angles mostly 137–144°. Conformer 3 has the shortest and most linear O–H···O contact; 17, 14, and 16 combine similarly good contacts with relatively unobstructed placement of the aziridine. Conformer 12 has excellent hydrogen-bond geometry but a more folded N/O region, making its exact placement less certain. 4. Conformers 2, 4, 28, 6, 22, 5, and 19 also contain clear O–H···O contacts, but these are generally longer, more bent, or accompanied by closer nonbonded approach of the aziridine to the alcohol region. Conformer 11 has a still more bent contact, while 25 has a relatively long O···O separation near 2.97 Å. 5. Conformer 30 has only a weak, bent O–H···O contact: H···O is about 2.40 Å and the donor–H–acceptor angle is near 122°, so it follows the well-formed hydrogen-bonded structures. 6. The remaining conformers lack a convincing O–H···O or O–H···N bond. Conformers 7 and 27 have weak, bent donor/acceptor approaches and therefore receive a small advantage. Among the fully non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 20, 26, 10, and 15 are comparatively open and avoid severe clashes. Conformers 18, 1, and especially 8 fold the nitrogen and alcohol oxygen into relatively close but poorly oriented contacts, giving acceptor/acceptor or badly aligned donor/acceptor proximity without compensating hydrogen bonding. 7. The middle of the ranking is uncertain because several O–H···O contacts differ by only a few hundredths of an angstrom and all structures appear geometrically reasonable. Solvation could also penalize the internally hydrogen-bonded conformers and substantially change this gas-phase-style estimate.

The molecule is acyclic, and the imidate headgroup has very similar local bond geometry in all structures, so the main differences are backbone torsions and intramolecular hydrogen bonding. Conformers 5, 9, 13, 8, 17, and 2 fold the terminal alcohol back toward the linker oxygen. The strongest O-H...O arrangements are in 5 and 9: O...O is about 2.80 Angstrom, H...O about 1.88-1.90 Angstrom, and the bonds are nearly linear. Conformer 13 has similarly favorable distances and directionality but requires more gauche backbone torsions. Conformer 8 remains a good hydrogen-bonded fold, with O...O about 2.92 and H...O about 2.02 Angstrom. The contacts in 17 and especially 2 are longer and more bent, so their hydrogen-bond stabilization is less certain; 17 benefits from one additional anti torsion relative to 2. Conformer 30 is the best non-hydrogen-bonded structure: it is the most extended backbone and has three of the four principal O-C-C-C/C-C-C-X torsions in anti-like arrangements, with no close nonbonded contacts. Conformers 3 and 1 have extended gauche-anti-anti-gauche backbones and are nearly equivalent. Conformers 26 and 12 also have two anti-like torsions and remain extended, while 11, 20, and 23 have two anti-like torsions but somewhat more folding; 23 contains a closer folded 1,5 contact near the alcohol end. Among structures with only one anti-like backbone torsion, 29/22 and 10/15 avoid the most unfavorable close contacts and are favored over the more compact 14/28 and 19/21 arrangements. Conformer 18 has a possible N-H...O(alcohol) contact, but H...O is about 2.45 Angstrom and the angle is bent, so it is only a weak compensation for its several gauche torsions. Conformer 24 is compact without a useful hydrogen bond. Conformers 27 and 4 are regular all-gauche helical arrangements with relatively separated oxygens, whereas 6, 7, 25, and 16 combine many gauche torsions with close, unsatisfied linker-O/alcohol-O approaches of roughly 3.35-3.52 Angstrom; 7 has a very weakly directed O-H...O approach, while 16 has the alcohol hydrogen directed away and is placed last. No severe atomic overlap or ring strain is evident, so orderings within the near-degenerate pairs 3/1, 26/12, 29/22, 10/15, 14/28, and 19/21 are especially uncertain, as is the boundary between weakly hydrogen-bonded 2 or 18 and the best extended conformers.

The heavy-atom sequence is N≡C–CH2–O–CH2–CH2–cyclopropyl. All conformers retain essentially the same cyclopropane geometry, so ring strain is nearly constant. There is no hydrogen-bond donor; therefore N and O cannot form a conventional intramolecular hydrogen bond, and the ranking is controlled mainly by ether/chain torsions, dipole alignment, weak C–H···N/O contacts, and steric contacts. I classified the three principal torsions as a = C(nitrile)–CH2–O–CH2, b = CH2–O–CH2–CH2, and c = O–CH2–CH2–C(cyclopropyl), with A denoting anti and G staggered gauche. The coordinate-derived families are GAA: 6,13; AAA: 16,30; GGA: 1,3,4,10,12; GAG: 7,15,18,22,24; AGA: 5,23,28; AAG: 17; AGG: 25; GGG: 11,14,19,20,26,29. Conformers 2,8,9,27 have c displaced to roughly 75–100 degrees rather than a normal staggered minimum, while 21 has b near 100 degrees. I give a modest preference to gauche a because an oxygen lone pair can align favorably with the electron-withdrawing CH2–CN bond (an α-cyano/anomeric-type gauche stabilization); ordinary b and c torsions favor anti because of reduced steric and eclipsing strain. Thus 6 and 13 combine the favorable α-cyano gauche arrangement with anti downstream bonds. Conformers 3 and 12 add only a well-separated b-gauche arrangement. The fully anti pair 16/30 is also very favorable and could interchange with 3/12 if the α-cyano gauche effect is weaker than estimated. Within GGA, 1 and 4 have a shorter approximately 3.1 Å nitrile-carbon-to-downstream-CH2 approach than 3/12, giving mild syn-pentane-like crowding; 10 additionally points both cyclopropane carbons toward the upstream CH2 at about 3.0–3.2 Å. The GAG structures avoid adjacent gauche bonds; 18/22 are more extended, whereas 7/24/15 fold the nitrile and ring ends somewhat closer without a severe clash. The fully gauche structures retain staggered local geometry, but incur two ordinary gauche penalties; 20/26 and 11/14 are more extended than 29/19, with 19 showing the strongest end-to-end folding. The anti-a families 5/23/28 and 17 lose the proposed α-cyano gauche stabilization, while 25 also contains two ordinary gauche torsions. Finally, 9,27,8,2 and especially 21 contain substantially skewed, partly eclipsed torsions; 2 also has the less favorable ring-facing geometry. Several mirror-related or sign-reversed pairs are effectively degenerate, especially 6/13, 16/30, 18/22, 1/4, 7/24, 20/26, and 11/14. The ordering within those pairs, and the relative placement of AAA versus low-strain GGA/GAG families, is correspondingly uncertain.

The heavy-atom connectivity defines a seven-membered unsaturated ether ring bearing a hydroxymethyl substituent at one alkene carbon. I first compared ring puckering and transannular crowding. Using ring order A-B-C-D-E-O-G, the least crowded twist-chair-like geometries generally have one moderate B···E contact near 2.9-3.0 Å and a more open D···G separation near 3.2 Å; this favors 9, 1, 14, 16 and, with a less favorable hydroxymethyl rotamer, 5, 4, 27, 6. A second low-strain family, including 20, 17, 26, 10, 22, 19, 18, 30 and 23, has B···E near 3.2 Å and D···G near 3.1 Å. The 11/29/7/13/15/3/25/28 family folds two methylene-rich portions closer, with D···G around 2.9 Å, so transannular H···H crowding is somewhat greater. The most compact family, 21, 2, 24, 8 and 12, has both relevant cross-ring distances short, including D···G near 2.8 Å, and was penalized for boat-like folding and less favorable torsional staggering. I next assessed hydroxymethyl orientation. In 20, 17, 26, 10, 16, 9, 1, 14, 11, 29, 7, 13, 15, 21 and 2, the alcohol oxygen remains relatively far from both neighboring ring directions, minimizing allylic steric compression. In 5, 4, 27, 6, 22, 19, 18, 3, 25, 24, 8 and 12 it approaches the saturated ring-side carbon at roughly 2.77-2.97 Å, giving a modest steric penalty; 12 is additionally unfavorable because its hydroxyl H points inward toward that region. In 23, 30 and especially 28, the alcohol oxygen approaches the vinylic side at about 2.75-2.93 Å, producing another compressed allylic rotamer. No conformer has a convincing strong O-H···O intramolecular hydrogen bond: alcohol-to-ring-oxygen separations are generally about 3.6-5 Å. Conformer 20 has the best weak approach, with H···O about 2.9 Å and an angle near 129 degrees, so it receives a small stabilization, but not enough to dominate ring strain. Within each geometric family, outward-pointing hydroxyl H atoms, longer nonbonded contacts and smoother staggered puckering were preferred. The ordering among adjacent members of the same family is uncertain because the expected differences are small and depend on subtle torsional and dipolar effects that cannot be quantified reliably from geometry alone.

1) The coordinates indicate a highly constrained fused small-ring core containing an ether oxygen. Across the set, the core bond lengths and puckering are broadly similar, with no conformer showing a uniquely catastrophic ring deformation; therefore side-chain torsions and nonbonded contacts dominate the estimate. 2) Conformers 9 and 16 have the only clear intramolecular O–H···O(ether) hydrogen bonds. For 9, H···O is about 2.00 Å, O···O about 2.93 Å, and the angle is approximately 163°; for 16 the corresponding values are about 2.06 Å, 2.95 Å, and 153°. Thus 9 is placed slightly ahead of 16, although they are a close pair. 3) Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 19, 22, 10, 14, 11, 25, 12, 23, and 24 have relatively extended, approximately anti O–C–C–C side chains, with O-to-ring-attachment distances around 3.7–3.8 Å. This reduces crowding between the hydroxymethyl terminus and the fused core. Within this group, 19, 22, and 10 direct the terminal carbon most cleanly away from the more substituted fused-ring branch; 23 and 24 retain somewhat closer terminal-carbon/core contacts and are ranked lower in the tier. 4) Conformers 27, 3, 30, 29, 28, and 2 have staggered gauche hydroxyl-chain torsions but still provide good clearance from the crowded fused-ring carbon, so they form the next tier. Conformers 4, 7, 20, and 8 have progressively smaller clearance to the secondary ring branch and are placed somewhat lower. 5) Conformers 1, 15, 21, 18, 17, 6, and 13 also use gauche side-chain arrangements, but the terminal carbon lies closer to the more substituted side of the bicyclic core, increasing gauche/steric interactions without compensating hydrogen bonding. 6) Conformers 5 and 26 have intermediate rather than cleanly staggered O–C–C–C geometries: their O-to-attachment distances are about 3.36 and 3.49 Å, respectively, consistent with appreciable torsional/eclipsing strain. They are therefore placed last, with 26 judged the more strongly eclipsed. Exact ordering within the non-hydrogen-bonded tiers is uncertain because the fused-core distortions and ordinary gauche penalties differ only subtly and no electronic energies are available.

The heavy-atom connectivity is a 1,3-disubstituted cyclobutane bearing a hydroxyethyl group and a ring alcohol. All structures retain reasonable bond lengths and broadly similar, mildly puckered cyclobutane geometries, so the main distinctions are intramolecular O-H...O bonding and side-chain torsions rather than gross ring strain or severe clashes. First, conformers 1, 30, 9, and 25 form clear intramolecular hydrogen bonds: their O...O distances are about 2.87, 2.88, 2.89, and 2.92 Å, respectively. In 1 and 30 the terminal alcohol donates to the ring oxygen with nearly linear geometry and H...O near 1.9 Å; 1 is marginally favored by its slightly tighter contact. In 9 and 25 the ring alcohol is the donor; 9 has the less bent and shorter contact, so it precedes 25. These hydrogen bonds should outweigh the folding and modest ring-flattening needed to form them. Among the non-hydrogen-bonded structures, 15, 23, 16, 18, 26, and 10 have especially extended, low-crowding side chains and an approximately anti O-C-C-ring arrangement, indicated by terminal-O to ring-attachment separations near 3.7-3.8 Å. Conformers 15, 23, and 16 also keep the two oxygens very widely separated, about 6.5 Å, while maintaining pseudo-equatorial substituent directions; they are therefore the best non-hydrogen-bonded set. Conformers 29, 20, 22, and 21 retain an extended carbon backbone and large O...O separation but use a less favorable terminal-alcohol gauche rotamer. The following group, 8, 4, 3, 6, 5, 19, 24, 27, 7, 2, and 14, is also free of serious clashes, but progressively brings the hydroxyl groups closer or adopts less favorable dipole/torsional orientations; their ordering is correspondingly subtle. Conformers 13, 28, 17, 11, and 12 place the side-chain carbon gauche to both adjacent ring bonds, folding the terminal carbinol toward the opposite side of the cyclobutane without obtaining a strong hydrogen bond. Conformer 13 partly compensates through an anti terminal-O torsion and wide O...O separation, while 28 is less extended. Conformers 17, 11, and especially 12 have relatively close oxygen pairs, about 4.26, 4.05, and 3.85 Å, but donor hydrogens point poorly for hydrogen bonding, leaving torsional cost and some oxygen-oxygen repulsion. Exact ordering outside the four hydrogen-bonded conformers is uncertain because ring-puckering and alcohol-rotamer energy differences are likely only a few tenths of a kcal/mol.

The common geometry is an aldehyde-containing chain followed by a C≡C unit and a terminal aziridine. The carbonyl, alkyne, and three-membered ring have essentially unchanged bond lengths and angles across the set, so their intrinsic bond and ring strain do not distinguish the conformers. No convincing intramolecular N–H···O hydrogen bond occurs: even the most folded structures have O···N distances around 4.5–4.9 Å and poorly positioned, substantially longer H···O contacts. The main energetic variables are therefore the two saturated-chain torsions, secondary nonbonded contacts generated by folding, and weak terminal dipole interactions. Conformers 1, 5, 14, 23, and 28 have both an extended central torsion and the carbonyl oxygen directed away from the beta-chain carbon; they avoid the gauche 1,4 interaction and form the lowest-strain group. Their internal differences are very small, so terminal O/N separation and absence of inward-directed contacts are only weak tie-breakers. Most of the remaining structures retain the favorable carbonyl orientation but have a gauche central C–C torsion, producing an approximately 3.0 Å carbonyl-carbon-to-alkyne-side 1,4 separation. Within that family, 25, 3, 9, 7, 19, 15, 8, and 21 are relatively open at the ends, whereas 26, 20, 12, 22, 10, 2, and 17 bring the terminal heteroatom dipoles somewhat closer; these distinctions should be much smaller than the anti-versus-gauche penalty. Conformers 4, 13, and 16 keep the central torsion extended but rotate the aldehyde into a less favorable orientation, shortening the carbonyl-O···beta-C contact to about 2.82 Å rather than roughly 3.55 Å. This local contact competes energetically with the ordinary central-chain gauche penalty, making their placement relative to the preceding gauche conformers uncertain. Conformers 18, 29, 27, and 11 have the favorable aldehyde orientation but a more inward combination of torsions, with the carbonyl oxygen only about 3.8 Å from the near alkyne carbon; 30 folds still further, with that distance near 3.6 Å and O···N near 4.6 Å. Finally, 24 and 6 combine a gauche central torsion with the short approximately 2.83 Å O···beta-C arrangement and an approximately 3.0 Å O···alkyne-side contact. They consequently have the strongest accumulated local crowding; 6 is slightly less favorable because its terminal O···N approach is also the shortest. The ordering inside each geometric family is low confidence because the relevant dispersion and dipole differences are small, but the separation into open anti, ordinary gauche, locally crowded carbonyl, and doubly folded classes is more robust.

The oxetane ring geometry is broadly similar throughout: all structures retain the expected nearly planar, strained four-membered ring, and none shows an obvious bond-angle distortion severe enough to dominate the ranking. The main discriminants are therefore substituent torsions and intramolecular O–H···O contacts. First, conformers 30, 23, and 11 contain genuine hydroxyl-to-carbonyl hydrogen bonds. Their H···O(carbonyl) distances are about 1.92, 1.94, and 2.04 Å, with O–H···O angles approximately 163°, 151°, and 146°, respectively. This makes 30 the clearest minimum; 23 has a stronger contact than 11 but a somewhat more folded/syn carbonyl geometry, so their separation is less certain. Second, conformers 28, 20, 17, 5, 13, 27, and 15 place the hydroxyl proton near the oxetane oxygen. These are geometrically constrained, bent five-membered contacts rather than ideal hydrogen bonds: H···O is roughly 2.15–2.27 Å but O–H···O is only about 109–113°. Within this group, 28, 20, 17, and 5 combine the contact with relatively extended, staggered aldehyde-side-chain geometries. Conformer 13 has the best local H···O geometry but a more folded side chain; 27 and 15 use more syn carbonyl torsions and are therefore placed somewhat lower. Conformers 16, 4, 10, and 1 have weaker hydroxyl/ether approaches, with O···O near 3.0 Å and H···O around 2.5–2.7 Å, but otherwise favorable extended, largely staggered chains. Conformers 26, 24, 25, 2, and 7 lack a useful hydrogen bond but are comparatively open and avoid serious heteroatom crowding; their relative ordering is especially uncertain because it depends mainly on small torsional, dipolar, and dispersion differences. Conformers 29, 9, and 6 retain weak ether-directed OH geometries but have less favorable folded or syn side-chain arrangements. Conformer 18 has an ether-directed OH contact, but the hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens are also only about 2.94 Å apart while the proton points away from the carbonyl, partly canceling the benefit. Conformer 12 is compact, with the carbonyl brought toward the ring region and a less favorable intermediate carbonyl torsion. Conformers 14 and 22 lack compensating hydrogen bonds and use syn carbonyl-side-chain arrangements; 3 is additionally compact around the carbonyl/ring-oxygen region. Finally, 21, 19, and 8 place hydroxyl and carbonyl oxygens at about 2.91, 2.86, and 2.84 Å without an O–H···O bridge, producing unfavorable acceptor–acceptor crowding. Conformer 8 is the least favorable because its hydroxyl oxygen is simultaneously close to the carbonyl and ring oxygens. Ordering within the broad non-hydrogen-bonded middle and lower tiers is uncertain and could readily shift by several positions with an electronic-structure calculation.

All structures retain essentially the same epoxide geometry, with no conspicuous bond-length distortion or unique ring opening; relative stability therefore depends mainly on side-chain torsions and intramolecular contacts. Conformers 13 and 17 have the clearest six-membered O–H···O=C contacts: H···O is about 1.84–1.86 Å, O···O about 2.74–2.76 Å, and the donor angle about 153–154°, making them the strongest candidates, with 13 marginally better. Conformers 8 and 23 also fold the alcohol toward the carbonyl, but their H···O distances are about 2.26–2.29 Å and angles only about 129–130°, so the stabilization is weaker. Conformer 21 has a short alcohol-to-epoxide contact (H···O about 2.00 Å, O···O about 2.64 Å), although its approximately 122° angle and constrained five-membered geometry keep it below the strongest carbonyl-bound pair. Conformers 2, 9, and 1 form N–H···O(epoxide) contacts; 2 is best at roughly 2.19 Å and 127°, followed by 9 and 1 near 2.25–2.28 Å and 121–122°. Conformers 22 and 14 have similar alcohol-to-epoxide contacts near 2.11 Å but more bent angles near 116°; 22 is favored slightly because the remaining heteroatoms are more separated. Conformers 28, 26, 20, and 30 retain progressively weaker, more bent O–H···O(epoxide) approaches (roughly 2.17–2.32 Å and 107–113°). Among conformers without a persuasive hydrogen bond, 25, 11, 16, and 12 place the carbonyl and epoxide oxygens relatively far apart and avoid strong folded clashes; 11 has a short but poorly directed N–H···O(alcohol) approach and is only slightly favored over the comparable open structures. Conformers 24, 6, 19, 10, 5, 15, 3, and 7 are broadly similar open rotamers and are ordered by the degree of heteroatom separation and avoidance of close epoxide/carbonyl or epoxide/amide contacts; differences within this group are small. Conformers 27, 29, 18, and 4 are increasingly compact without a well-directed compensating hydrogen bond.
